review_scope: Recurring treehouse/garden/pond/plaza/courtyard views and the distinct neighborhood path, including closing-theme shots. Image hashes identify pixels actually inspected; production landmarks are not new prose canon.

review_policy.hash_rule: Any pixel change invalidates the old visual review until a reviewer inspects the replacement and records its new hash.
review_policy.authority_rule: Source facts come from revision/latest.md and author references. Production landmarks are choices frozen for cross-shot continuity, not dimensions or history invented for the prose.
review_policy.reference_rule: A changed canonical reference invalidates dependent image reviews even if their own pixels did not change.

locations.name: Maia's garden oak and shared treehouse

source_facts.anchor: The treehouse was built high among the sturdy branches of an old oak
The hollow underneath the structure had a second secret entrance

canonical_references.role: Author repository reference: old oak, raised room, ladder and lower hollow.
Governing production interior: governing room layout.
Governing production exterior derived from the interior.

invariants.text: One old oak with sturdy load-bearing branches and a thick canopy, in the far corner of Maia's garden; distinct from the Tree of Echoes.
A raised main room reached by an old ladder, and a separate lower hollow with a second secret entrance; the lower entrance does not replace the upper room.
Patched timber, a wooden roof beneath the canopy, open window cutouts with scrap-fabric curtains, maps/drawings, cushions, blankets, a small wooden table and treasure boxes.
In the garden-wide camera, the broad upper room projects left of the massive right-hand trunk; its arched upper entrance is at the trunk/right end.
The ladder connects the lower refuge to an opening in the upper landing beside the arched upper door. Door, landing and room floor occupy one connected upper level.
The canonical garden-wide view has a broad rounded lower seating platform surrounding the hollow: cushions, low tables, maps and chests. Beds border this refuge; they do not replace its floor.

In the canonical interior camera, the massive diagonal trunk is left, the arched door behind it near center-left, and open viewing bays/branch rails/curtains extend across the right. The initial low round map table sits near the right foreground; later furniture and dressing may change while retaining coherent access and support.

Weather and later-time variants preserve the room's structural shell and connected access: trunk, door, beams, open viewing bays and rails stay coherent. Weather and light must be visibly distinct where the scene requires it; no glazing is added. Furniture, cushions, papers and other lived-in dressing may move or accumulate across years and must not be frozen in identical positions solely for pixel consistency.
Keep one consistent human-usable room, door, ladder and landing. A new camera may foreshorten them, but must not turn the upper room into a tiny trunk cupboard or a detached cottage.
An image assigned to the canonical garden approach cannot add a new cluster of cottage-like tree buildings or a bridge route in place of the established ground path.

The early shaded room, rainy refuge and later remembrance state must show readable outdoor/light/weather differences and appropriate lived-in changes across the intervening years. Reusing an architectural shell is not a requirement to repeat all furniture and exterior appearance.

views.description: Ground path looking toward the oak and both levels.
Inside the upper room looking past the trunk to the door and open viewing bays.
A close view within the same upper room; landmarks outside the crop need not be visible.
At the actual upper entrance reached by the ladder, with a connected safe landing and clear access into the broad room.

locations.name: Maia's planting beds and ground paths

source_facts.anchor: one of my favorite activities was spending time in Maia's garden

canonical_references.role: Garden-to-oak relationship when the treehouse is visible.

invariants.text: Maia tends a varied garden with flowers, insects, places for planting and ponds. Different beds and light levels may appear; individual plant positions are not prose canon.
The established approach is a gently curving ground-level stone path through timber-edged beds, within an enclosed planted garden. It is not a newly invented elevated bridge neighborhood.
Planting activities take place on broad dry ground; pots and tools stay within reach. Standing or kneeling people have support on the bank/path, not on water.
Sheltered foliage, tactile wood/stone, and local natural-looking/artificial daylight with small warm light sources. No exposed space panorama before the story's reveal.

views.description: Local planting bed or garden detail; distant layout may be outside the frame.
A person-sized ground path through the established beds.

canonical_references.role: Governing basin geometry: shallow water, low coping and adjacent dry ground.

invariants.text: Lyra's fall is into a shallow small pond; Cali and Kael help her to its edge. The water-wheel project is later placed in one of the garden ponds.
These selected shots reuse one visual pond for economy; the manuscript does not specify that every pond event occurs at exactly one named basin.
Preserve the low irregular stone basin, shallow visible pebbles, timber boundary/fence, plants and accessible bank from garden-pond.png.
Use the dry stone working bank established by garden-work-area.png. No full-body standing cast on the narrow rim or water surface.
During the rescue Lyra is wet and frightened; rescuers crouch on supported dry ground and reach her naturally. The recovery takes place on the dry bank beside the same water.
The wheel is a miniature handmade project built by children with Arin's guidance; it is not a mill building or full-sized mechanism.

The governing garden-pond view establishes a low basin beside adjacent dry ground. Across views preserve the waterline-to-coping-to-paving vertical relationship; camera angle alone cannot turn it into a raised retaining-wall pool.

Compare the visible near/far basin arcs, coping thickness, side returns and at least three shared anchors where visible against garden-pond.png. Any difference must admit a coherent camera/depth explanation. Cropped-out features remain unobserved; plausible local figure contacts do not prove global geometry.

Within these shared-basin depictions, all visible water patches must connect plausibly to the same basin. Do not leave an isolated far water strip behind a dry bank that implies another pool; any peninsula or occlusion needs a coherent visible shoreline explanation.
